transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I suppose... well, it's about my driving. I still drive myself everywhere, you know. I have a beautiful old Buick, the seats are so plush, not like these stiff new cars my daughter drives. She’s always telling me I should give up my keys, but I told her, 'I have a college degree, I think I know how to handle a sedan.' 

But... well, what finally made me come in today is that the moment my car reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami, my chest just tightens up terribly. My hands clamp down on the steering wheel, and I get this sudden, overwhelming certainty that I have to get off right then and there, even though there’s nowhere to go. You’re just stuck up there over the water. 

And speaking of Miami, I really don't even know why people want to go down there so much anymore. I remember going in the seventies and it was lovely, you could actually find a parking spot near the shops. Now it's just all construction and people driving like absolute maniacs. I went to a restaurant down there last year and they charged me six dollars for a cup of black coffee! Can you believe that? But yes, anyway... those bridges. I just get that awful feeling.
Doctor: Have you ever had similar feelings of chest tightness and overwhelming anxiety in other situations, or does this only happen when you're driving on bridges?

No, no, it's really just the bridges. I don't get that feeling anywhere else. My chest is perfectly fine otherwise. I actually just saw my regular doctor for my checkup last month, and he said my heart is in wonderful shape. He always tells me I'm going to outlive him! He’s a very nice young man, though he does mumble quite a bit. 

Honestly, young people today just do not enunciate. When I was getting my degree, they actually expected you to speak clearly if you wanted to be taken seriously. Now everyone is just looking down at those little phones, mumbling and typing away with their thumbs. I saw a girl walk right into a light pole the other day at the Publix parking lot! Just smacked right into it because she couldn't be bothered to look up from her screen. And don't even get me started on the prices at that Publix. They want almost five dollars for a carton of eggs now! Can you imagine? 

But... oh, what were we saying? Right, my chest. No, I don't panic at the grocery store or driving around town or anywhere else. I feel perfectly fine in my car normally. It is just when I get stuck up high over that water.
When you feel that overwhelming need to get off the bridge, is it because you're worried something bad might happen to you, like a panic attack, or because you feel trapped with no way to escape?

Well, it’s not really about having a... a medical episode or anything like that. It’s just... I know perfectly well those bridges are safe. They’ve been there for years and years, and plenty of people cross them every single day without a second thought. But when I'm up there, and I think about driving over all that open water... the fear I get just feels so much bigger than the actual danger. It's completely out of proportion, I know that in my head. 

It's just all that water down there. My husband, God rest his soul, he used to absolutely love the water. He had this little aluminum fishing boat when we first moved down here. Oh, it was nothing fancy, but we used to take it out on the weekends. Of course, that was before the marinas started charging an arm and a leg just to tie your boat to a dock. We used to pay, I think, maybe twenty-five dollars a month for a slip? Now my neighbor tells me they want hundreds of dollars! Hundreds! For a wet piece of wood! And the pelicans just ruin the paint on your boat anyway, they make an absolute mess of everything. The city doesn't do a thing about it, either. I wrote a very polite letter to the mayor about the bird droppings at the community park, and do you think I got a real reply? Just a printed form letter from some secretary. They don't care about the residents anymore, just the tourists. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, the bridges. Yes, it's just that feeling that the water is so big and the danger feels so huge, even though my sensible mind knows the bridge isn't going to just fall down.
